title: Template escaping - the Blade {{ }} idea in plain PHP
answer: Blade's {{ $name }} prints a value escaped for HTML, and {!! $html !!} prints it raw. In plain PHP, htmlspecialchars is the same protection. Always escape in the view, at the moment of printing, and keep raw output for trusted HTML only.
pitfall: Marking user input as trusted HTML is the fastest way to an XSS hole. Only content your own code generated may skip escaping.

title: Eloquent-style queries explained in plain PDO
answer: Eloquent-style code chains methods like where and orderBy to build a query, then get runs it. Underneath, it still becomes SQL with bound parameters. The plain-PDO version below shows exactly what the chain means, so the magic is never mysterious. This example is syntax-checked only because it needs a database and a $pdo object.
pitfall: Chaining where calls inside a loop can fire one query per row, the N+1 problem. Fetch related data in one query with a join or eager loading instead.

title: Middleware concept - wrapping requests with auth and logging
answer: Middleware is a layer that runs before or after the handler: check login, log the request, or add headers. Each layer either passes the request onward or returns a response early, such as a redirect to login. This example is syntax-checked only because it models request flow.
pitfall: Middleware that forgets to call the next handler silently drops the request. Every path must either return a response or call the next layer.

title: MVC pattern in plain PHP - Model, View, Controller without a framework
answer: MVC separates concerns: the Model talks to the database, the Controller handles the request and picks data, and the View only prints HTML. Even without a framework, keeping these apart makes code testable and readable. This example is syntax-checked only because it models request flow, not a runnable script.
pitfall: Putting SQL queries inside view files mixes layers and makes the page untestable. Views should receive ready data and only escape and print it.

title: Routing in plain PHP - a tiny router with methods and parameters
answer: A router maps a method plus a path to a handler. Match the request method and URI, pull {id} segments out of the path, and return a 404 for anything unmatched. This example is syntax-checked only because it needs an HTTP request.
pitfall: Matching routes with plain string equality breaks on trailing slashes and query strings. Normalise the path first, and strip the query part before matching.
